title: Purpose and long life
hookLine: people with a sense of purpose tended to live longer in a large study

cards: Somewhere on a long questionnaire sits a quiet question. Roughly: do you have a sense of direction in your life, or do you mostly drift?
Thousands of American adults answered questions like that, along with many others about their health and their days. Then the researchers did something patient. They waited.
Years later, they checked the records to see who was still alive. What the waiting turned up about purpose is worth hearing slowly, without rounding it up.

teach.b: The psychologists Patrick Hill and Nicholas Turiano reported in the journal Psychological Science that people with a stronger sense of purpose were less likely to die over the years of the study, even after accounting for other factors they had measured.
Second, the surprise. The link wasn't only for older people.
It showed up among younger, middle-aged and older adults alike. Purpose isn't just a question for retirement. Third, the caution.

Nobody was assigned a purpose; people simply reported how they felt about their lives. Purpose can travel with other things, like good health, steady work or close friends, and a questionnaire can't fully pull them apart.
So the study supports a link. It doesn't promise that finding a purpose will add years to anyone's life. Fourth, purpose up close.
The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote his notebooks to himself, and one entry starts with a very ordinary struggle: not wanting to get out of bed.

teach.h: THE WORK OF A HUMAN BEING.
teach.b: His answer, in George Long's translation: "I am rising to the work of a human being." Not a grand mission. Just the ordinary work of being a person, done on purpose.
The purpose people reported in the study wasn't measured in size either. It was a sense of direction.

how: Some contemplative and philosophical traditions ask people to name what they live for; some people write a single sentence of purpose and return to it each morning or evening.

games.q: what does “purpose and long life” mean?
o: the plan for retirement you make in your sixties
a sense of direction, linked in one study with longer life
a big life goal that is proven to add years

games.q: purpose and long life: tap the pairs.
p: the work of a human being

s: the link between purpose and long life showed up only in older people
it appeared among younger, middle-aged and older adults alike.
the study shows that finding a purpose will add years to your life

Marcus Aurelius wrote about not wanting to get out of bed
his answer to himself: "I am rising to the work of a human being."

games.q: you're Marcus Aurelius. it's morning, and you don't want to get up. what do you tell yourself?
o: "I am rising to the work of a human being."
"I'll get up when I feel like it."
games.why: he reminds himself what he's for: the ordinary work of being a person. not a grand mission, just a direction.

practice: Let a sentence begin, I'm here to, and see what finishes it, small enough to be true this week: to raise a kind kid, to make good bread, to tell the truth at work, to look after my mother.
If several come, keep the one that feels most like yours; if nothing comes, sitting with the question counts.

wordCard.voice: Purpose and long life. In one long study, a sense of direction went with a longer life. A link worth knowing, not a promise. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: purpose. Not a master plan, just a direction for the day. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.ref: Hill, P. L., and Turiano, N. A., "Purpose in life as a predictor of mortality across adulthood," Psychological Science (2014)
